item.title: What Does PTSD Sound Like?
item.description:
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder

What Does PTSD Sound Like?

How trauma alters auditory processing.

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • Sensory dysregulation is a central feature of PTSD, not simply a secondary consequence.
  • PTSD can impair auditory filtering, making irrelevant sounds difficult to suppress.
  • Trauma can alter how sounds are assigned threat, salience, and emotional meaning.
  • Auditory processing in PTSD can shift from sensory hyperreactivity to sensory shutdown.

Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is usually conceptualized in terms of its psychological impact. But Van der Kolk and McFarlane recently reminded us that beneath this affective/cognitive layer is a fundamental disruption in how the brain processes the sensory world.

In their article, they note that "little attention has been paid to the central role of sensory processing", that "critical elements of the phenomenology and neurobiology of traumatic stress" have been ignored, and that "somatic symptoms and lack of sensory regulation are central, not peripheral, to the clinical presentation of PTSD" [1].

With this in mind, we decided to ask the somewhat peculiar question: What does PTSD sound like?

To find out, we examined over 200 first-person accounts of sound and hearing from public PTSD communities. From these, we identified four canonical features that can be tethered to specific findings from auditory neuroscience in PTSD populations.

Auditory Disinhibition

  • "Background noise never becomes background. I hear all of it."*
  • “I hear everything, all at once, and my brain doesn't decide what I don't need to hear.”
  • "Every little sound gets my attention. Nothing seems to get filtered out."

Normally, the brain performs a remarkable audiological task — not hearing.

Repetitive, irrelevant sounds are suppressed so attention can be directed toward what matters — a process called sensory gating. In PTSD, this system can become less effective, leaving far more of the auditory environment competing for attention. This is not simply heightened sensitivity to sound, but a collapse of the distinction between what should be heard and what should be filtered.

Perhaps the most striking finding across the literature is the consistency of subjective sensory gating deficits, despite considerable heterogeneity in where the processing failure occurs. Across electrophysiological studies, PTSD is associated with weaker filtering of repetitive or irrelevant sounds, heightened automatic attention to unexpected auditory changes, and reduced inhibitory control over sensory processing. At the same time, the brain appears to preferentially process salient or emotionally meaningful information while giving less priority to neutral input [2–5].

In PTSD, the auditory baseline is cacophony.

Auditory Threat Reactivity

  • "A door slams and my whole body jumps before I even know what happened."
  • "A knock at the door can send my heart racing instantly."
  • "I still jump at loud noises every time — no matter how many times I remind myself I'm safe.”

The auditory system doesn't wait for conscious recognition before mounting a defensive response. Fast subcortical pathways route sudden sound straight to brainstem startle circuitry, while the amygdala regulates how strongly the body reacts — which is why a jolt, a racing heart, or a surge of adrenaline can arrive before the sound has even been identified [6, 7].

In PTSD, this reflex isn't simply turned up across the board. It's especially sensitive to context: Startle responses become most abnormal specifically under unpredictable threat, which is why the same sound can barely register one day and set off a full reaction the next, depending on stress, perceived safety, and expectation [8]. The body responds to sound before the mind can decide if it's dangerous.

In PTSD, the fear circuit turns up the gain on an auditory startle reflex.

Conditioned Auditory Salience

  • “The sound of dishes being handled aggressively makes me freeze. It used to come right before an argument.”
  • “Whenever I hear a hint of frustration in someone’s voice, I immediately start bracing for what comes next.”
  • “A car pulling into the driveway still makes me tense. That sound used to mean they were home.”

In PTSD, the importance of a sound may have surprisingly little to do with its volume. Through fear conditioning, an otherwise ordinary sound can acquire predictive meaning because it was repeatedly associated with danger [6].

The effect is especially interesting with the human voice. Studies of affective prosody, the emotional information carried by tone and rhythm rather than words, find altered processing in PTSD [9]. In women with childhood-abuse-related PTSD, identification of several emotional tones was slowed, while recognition of anger was relatively preserved, suggesting preferential processing of threat-relevant vocal information [10].

This may also explain why predictability and control matter so much. PTSD studies find particularly abnormal responses to unpredictable threat [8] and impaired use of contextual safety signals [11]. The auditory system is responding not simply to how loud a sound is, but to what that sound has been learned to mean.

Just as the body keeps the score, so does the ear.

Dissociative Auditory Attenuation

  • "People are talking to me, but suddenly their voices sound far away."
  • "Everything becomes muffled, like I'm hearing it underwater."
  • "I can see someone speaking, but the words stop registering."

PTSD can present along two broad response patterns: a hyperaroused presentation, in which threat-response systems remain highly engaged, and a dissociative presentation, characterized by greater shutdown and disengagement.

Interestingly, auditory processing appears to track this divide. In combat veterans, intrusive re-experiencing was associated with larger neural responses to startling sounds, while maladaptive avoidance was associated with reduced neural responses to the same sounds [12]. The auditory system in PTSD, then, is not simply turned up. Its regulation can move in either direction, from sensory flooding to sensory shutdown.

In PTSD, psychology and neurobiology are coupled.

What PTSD Sounds Like

Taken together, these accounts support a broader idea now emerging in PTSD research: Sensory dysregulation is not simply a byproduct of PTSD, but part of the disorder itself. Understanding PTSD requires asking not only what happened, how it is remembered, and what it means, but also how that experience has changed the way the brain processes the sensory world.

This becomes especially important when PTSD occurs alongside disorders such as tinnitus and hyperacusis, where the auditory system is already central to the patient’s symptoms. At our tinnitus clinic, trauma-informed care means addressing both the psychological and auditory-processing elements of PTSD. It means that, in addition to the psychiatric history, we need to ask: What does the world sound like to you?

*These are composite examples, not direct quotes, in order to preserve the anonymity of the individuals whose experiences informed them.

item.title: The Hidden Problem With Positive Thinking
item.description:
Motivation

The Hidden Problem With Positive Thinking

Sometimes, imagining success can block you from achieving your goals.

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • Positive fantasies can feel motivating while actually reducing the effort you make.
  • Believing a goal is achievable is very different from imagining you've already achieved it.
  • Self-confidence helps you the most when it's paired with a realistic view of obstacles and difficulties.
  • With mental contrasting, you can connect a positive view of your future to the steps necessary to get there.

You have an important interview coming up, and you need to prepare. So you spend twenty minutes imagining yourself walking into the office looking great, impressing everyone you speak to, and immediately getting the job. The visualization is easy because you’ve already scripted it, too: To firm it up in your mind, you wrote out a detailed narrative of how much you impressed your interviewers. And this morning, just after you brushed your teeth, you looked yourself in the eye and declared, “I have everything I need to win, and my success is inevitable.” You repeated this fifteen times. As you drive to the interview, you’re feeling great — although a nagging voice in the corner of your awareness is asking you why you haven’t looked over your resume, even once.

Source: Image created by ChatGPT

But you mean to manifest success, no matter what, even if some people might call it delusional — delulu is the solulu, you once heard. So as you wait to be called in to the interview room, you browse a couple of TikToks about visualizing your financial future. You can imagine quite a bit of wealth. It’s a lot more fun doing that than explaining your departure from your last job, or the gap in your employment history — and less of a drag than doing research into the company you’re applying to. Of course it is; dwelling on potential problems could just drag you down, you think, as you stand up to meet your interviewer.

OK, end of scenario. I’ve painted with a pretty broad brush, so it’s easy to see that the “you” character above is leaving quite a lot on the table. In the example, “you” are full to the brim with optimism or ambition. It’s a form of motivation that other people will probably notice immediately, and it might be a really good look — at least at first. You’re trying to manifest good fortune — to use focused belief to bring something positive into the world.

And you can learn a lot about manifestation on social media. In 2025, an article in Religion Compass reported that TikToks about it had accumulated more than 62.8 billion views in the preceding few years. If you’ve been watching, you might have been encouraged to use affirmations (talking to yourself in the mirror), scripting (writing a story about your success, as if it has already happened), or vision boards (cutting-and-pasting images of things you want). Manifestation also informs “lucky girl syndrome” (repeating mantras about your own good fortune) as well as the more recent idea of the “17-second rule,” which claims that holding a positive thought in your mind for seventeen uninterrupted seconds can activate its power.

All of these techniques involve positive fantasies — efforts to experience the future you want, as if it’s real already — but, as Oettingen and Mayer pointed out in a 2002 paper, those positive fantasies aren’t the same as positive expectations. When you have positive expectations, you’re telling yourself that your goal is achievable — that you can do it. According to Oettingen & Mayer, believing this can help motivate you to put forth more effort and to try harder to achieve your goal, while simply fantasizing about the goal itself was associated with less effort and worse outcomes. In other words, when you believe something is possible, you’re more likely to work for it, but believing that you’ll achieve your goal no matter what doesn’t encourage any extra effort.

Why would imagining success make it less likely that you’ll prepare for it? Because creating a vivid mental picture of your outcome may help you experience, at least temporarily, some of the great feelings associated with goal attainment. Imagine yourself in a bigger office, after you get the promotion. Imagine getting an A because you’ve aced the exam. Imagine seeing the results of a deliberate change to your diet — you’ve managed to lose the weight, or to gain it. Although these images and fantasies might be pleasant to indulge in, research suggests that they might actually reduce the motivation to try as hard as you can. In a 2011 experiment, Kappes & Oettingen found that participants who fantasized about their futures put less energy into a task than participants in control conditions.

The central idea of “manifestation culture” thus seems to be that success will happen just because you think about it, which isn’t miles away from telling yourself that actual, real-world effort doesn’t matter. The research on manifestation, however, tells a different story. A 2025 study by Dixon et al. found that strong manifestation-related beliefs were associated with greater perceived success and aspirations, but also with a greater willingness to take risks — and even with bankruptcy. Maybe manifestation will increase your confidence as it helps you perceive success in detail, but what happens after your visualization is complete? If you’re making risky bets with your money, you’re leaving yourself more vulnerable to a loss.

But there is a more practical way to incorporate visualization into your striving for success. It’s called mental contrasting, and it incorporates manifesting your desired outcome in addition to envisioning the obstacles that stand between you and that outcome. As Gabriele Oettingen puts it: First, ask yourself what you want and what it would feel like to achieve it; then, identify and acknowledge the barriers or challenges in your way. Envision your positive future alongside those obstacles, as a kind of contrast. To accomplish X, you’ll have to get through Y. Then, make a decision about how to act on that obstacle. In so doing, you’re firming up your motivation and commitment to a useful, strategic course of action, and you’re activating the practical problem-solving side of your brain. So, while positive fantasies alone can sap your motivation, strategic and balanced fantasies may help you aim your energy in the right direction.

So it’s not that positive thinking, or envisioning a great future, is a problem on its own — it only becomes counterproductive when it draws your attention away from the path you’ll take to get to that future. Don’t stop picturing your goals, and don’t give up believing in yourself. As you visualize success, though, make sure that you spend at least as much time thinking and strategizing about what might get in your way. Instead of picturing tomorrow’s interview as an automatic lock — a job you’ll definitely, definitely get — remind yourself that you do have a genuine chance to get it, and ask yourself what you realistically have to do to get ready.

item.title: Why Work Doesn’t Need a Mission to Be Meaningful
item.description:
Career

Why Work Doesn’t Need a Mission to Be Meaningful

Engagement can emerge from more than social purpose.

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • Meaningful work is often framed too narrowly in contemporary workplace discussions.
  • Foundational engagement theory never limited meaningfulness to social purpose alone.
  • Work can become engaging through challenge, mastery, autonomy, and growth.
  • Work doesn’t have to “change the world” to feel psychologically worthwhile.
Source: ChatGPT 5.5

Last month, I discussed why total compensation is only weakly tied to work engagement. A major part of that argument was that work engagement shouldn’t be confused with job satisfaction; instead, it reflects a deeper form of psychological investment in the work itself.

Given that argument, it may seem surprising that I would push back against a claim made recently in an article on TriNet: that engagement ultimately comes down to performing meaningful work. The article, like many contemporary discussions of the topic, positioned meaningfulness largely in terms of workers contributing to “something bigger than themselves.”

And to be clear, a social- and purpose-oriented form of meaningfulness can absolutely foster engagement (Wrzesniewski et al., 1997). Teachers, healthcare workers, nonprofit employees, counselors, clergy, and many others may derive substantial engagement from the belief that their work genuinely matters in a broader social or moral sense.

The problem, however, is the embedded assumption that work cannot be meaningful (and therefore engaging) unless it carries some broader existential, social, or moral significance. And that's exactly what I want to push back on here.

Meaning Doesn’t Have to Be Mission-Driven

Although it’s easy to default to broader social or existential purpose as a source of meaning, the foundational work on engagement never defined meaningfulness in such narrow terms. In fact, in his influential work on engagement, Kahn (1990) described psychological meaningfulness as a “return on investments of self” in work role performance (p. 705). As such, meaningfulness wasn’t limited to social contribution, moral purpose, or organizational mission. Instead, people often experienced meaningfulness through challenge, growth, creativity, accomplishment, or rewarding interpersonal interactions.

That’s a somewhat different way of thinking about meaningful work. The question doesn't have to be about whether the work serves some larger purpose. It’s whether investing yourself in the work feels worthwhile. Those can certainly overlap, but they don’t have to. Someone may find work worthwhile because it helps other people or contributes to a cause they care about. Someone else may find it worthwhile because the work is difficult, interesting, allows them to exercise judgment, or gives them the satisfaction of becoming exceptionally good at something.

Consider a software engineer absorbed in solving a difficult technical problem, a musician trying to master a challenging piece, or an athlete working to improve some aspect of performance. There may be larger purposes attached to any of those activities, but there don’t have to be. The immediate experience of doing the activity can itself provide a reason to invest attention, effort, and parts of oneself in it.

That nuance shifts the focus away from what the work ultimately contributes to and toward what people experience while doing it. And if we accept that shift, there are several psychological mechanisms that can help explain why seemingly ordinary work can become engaging.

Engagement Reflects Psychological Need Fulfillment

One useful way to think about this comes from self-determination theory, developed by Deci and Ryan (1985). The theory proposes that people are more intrinsically motivated when three core psychological needs are fulfilled: autonomy, competence, and relatedness.

  • Autonomy reflects the desire to experience some degree of ownership, agency, or control over one’s work.
  • Competence reflects the desire to feel effective, capable, challenged, and able to develop mastery.
  • Relatedness reflects the desire to feel connected to and valued by other people.

Work that fulfills those needs can become deeply psychologically engaging even when the work itself is not especially purpose-driven or socially consequential. In fact, a recent meta-analysis found that satisfying these basic psychological needs is associated with a broad range of adaptive workplace outcomes, including work engagement (Hagger & McAnally Star, 2026).

This means work doesn't have to feel socially transformative in some grand sense to provide people with something psychologically valuable. It can give them opportunities to make choices, apply or develop their skills and abilities, or build meaningful relationships with others.

And that broader framing is important because contemporary discussions of meaningful work often drift toward a kind of implicit moral hierarchy in which socially beneficial or purpose-driven work is treated as inherently more meaningful than other forms of work. But psychologically speaking, meaningfulness is often far more subjective and multifaceted than that. People can derive deep meaning in lots of different ways, even when the work itself is not obviously world-changing.

There’s No Single Path to Meaningful Work

By this point, hopefully it’s obvious that there’s no single path to meaningful work. People become psychologically invested in all sorts of activities for all sorts of reasons. Sometimes that investment emerges from helping others or contributing to a broader mission. But sometimes it emerges from autonomy or craftsmanship or competition or simply the satisfaction of doing something well.

I'm not trying to diminish the importance of work that genuinely does serve broader social or moral purposes. But I am arguing that contemporary discussions of meaningfulness often frame the concept far too narrowly. Work doesn’t become psychologically worthwhile only when it changes the world, advances a moral cause, or contributes to “something bigger.” Sometimes meaningfulness is far more personal, experiential, and immediate than that.

And the reason that's important is because, as I argued recently, organizations often attempt to cultivate engagement through mission-oriented messaging, value statements, or purpose narratives, all the while overlooking the everyday characteristics of work that make psychological investment more likely in the first place. Work that allows people to experience competence, autonomy, or relatedness can become deeply engaging even when the broader societal significance of the work itself is relatively modest.

Meaningfulness, in other words, isn't a single thing. And work doesn’t have to save the world to feel worth investing in.

item.title: Are We Talking Too Much in Therapy?
item.description:
Trauma

Are We Talking Too Much in Therapy?

Personal Perspective: Getting to the bottom of "bottom-up therapy."

Posted September 23, 2026

Source: Sam Louie

It’s taken me a long time to arrive at this point of healing. I started therapy more than twenty years ago while going through a divorce. Over the years, I worked with individual and group therapists, attended a 12-Step program, church, and men’s groups, participated in workshops and trainings, and read hundreds of books on trauma, addiction, and healing. I understood my trauma “by chapter and verse.” Yet I was often cut off from the emotions. Much of my change remained intellectual.

I knew I had abandonment and rejection issues, addictions to address, feelings of inadequacy, cultural and language barriers in relating to my first-generation Chinese immigrant parents, and a sharp tongue that had once protected me from racist taunts and mockery. Eventually, I resigned myself to being “traumatized,” and felt my growth was as good as it gets.

Things began shifting when I experimented with my “right brain.” I used poetry, photography, drawing, and even childhood TV theme songs to access emotions. Sometimes I cried without knowing why. I began to recognize what art therapists have known for decades: We sometimes need to give the intellectual, explaining side of ourselves a break from reflexively talking:

“Words alone are not enough to make it happen. Recovery requires creative expression in symbol and metaphor.” —Cohen, Barnes, and Rankin, 1995

As I put images to words, my need to explain my past diminished. My longings, hurts, and fears began spilling onto the page through pictures. Hamel (2021) explains, “Traumatic memories stored as images in the right brain become accessible through drawing and painting.”

Source: Sam Louie

I also discovered sandplay therapy, which encouraged me to create scenes using miniature figures and objects rather than simply explaining my concerns. It helped me slow down my logical brain and experience what I had previously only been able to describe.

This distinction between “top-down” and “bottom-up” processing became increasingly meaningful. Bottom-up approaches intentionally bring attention to what is happening inside the body—sensations, images, emotions, impulses, gestures, and other experiences that may exist outside conscious awareness.

Around the time of COVID, I read No Bad Parts, which transformed how I understood myself. Internal Family Systems (IFS) helped me view my reactivity, anger, addictions, and compulsions not as “bad,” but as parts of me that had developed for protective reasons.

I began experimenting with this approach with my lifelong nail-biting habit. Instead of shaming the behavior, I became curious about its positive intention. As I listened internally, memories surfaced of being scared and home alone with my younger brothers while our parents worked. The nail-biting part had taken over to help me feel safe.

I was stunned. I had talked extensively about the fear growing up but had compartmentalized it as “a thing from my past.” I felt I had moved beyond it because I had no emotion around it. Little did I know, I was simply disconnected from the fear.

As Morgan (2015) explains, “Body signals are usually missed when attention is in outer, task-focused mode or sufficient time is not given.”

This helped me realize that simply talking about the past isn't always enough. We can know our history without fully experiencing or integrating it. In therapy today, I often slow down when clients tell their stories. Rather than immediately asking another question, I might ask, “As you’re talking about this, can you tell me what you’re noticing happening inside?”

The answer might be a physical sensation, image, sound, memory, symbol, emotion, or words. By slowing down, clients may access experiences that were previously outside their awareness.

The goal isn't simply to revisit painful memories. These approaches can create a new experience in the present—a corrective emotional experience that provides something the person needed but didn't receive.

As van der Kolk (2014) writes, “Trauma is primarily remembered not as a story, a narrative with a beginning, middle, and end, but as isolated sensory imprints.”

I initially believed therapy would “cure” my anxiety and addictions. I wanted freedom from rejection, inadequacy, and compulsive behaviors. What I’ve learned is that I’m really seeking integration. I’m still a work in progress, but I’m beginning to experience healing not just intellectually, but from the inside out.

Ironically, this inward focus was reiterated not only in therapy books but also in books about martial arts: “Most people live at a comfortable distance from their bodies since they pay hardly any attention to them… As humans, we spend so much time inside our heads that we often forget the way out.” —Bolelli, 2008

After all these years, my head and heart are finally beginning to connect. I'm learning healing in therapy isn't so much about talking more as it is about slowing down enough to notice what is happening within as I talk and share my stories,

item.title: “Don't Make Illness Your Identity": What Does Research Say?
item.description:
Chronic Illness

“Don't Make Illness Your Identity": What Does Research Say?

Is “Don’t let illness define you” good advice?

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • The phrase “Don’t make illness your identity” is controversial in the chronic illness community.
  • Illness impacts many aspects of our identity, but how we relate to it affects how we manage the challenges.
  • Four types of illness identity are: engulfment, rejection, acceptance, and enrichment.
  • The best outcomes are associated with acceptance and enrichment.
Source: Mikhail Nilov / Pexels

The phrases “Don’t make illness your identity” and “Don’t let illness define you” are controversial in the chronic illness community, and for good reason. On one hand, the phrases are often said by individuals who have no concept of what it’s like to live with illness every day—something that undoubtedly impacts your identity. On the other hand, we know it’s important to continue to foster all parts of our identity, even when illness takes up too much of our energy.

Another key tension with this phrase is that the acceptance of illness—which often requires a change in identity—is incredibly beneficial because it allows someone living with chronic illness to make aligned decisions and take appropriate actions that will support their current body.

So how do we approach illness with acceptance while also leaving room for other aspects of our identity? What does it even mean to have an illness identity?

What does the research actually say about illness identity?

Van Bulck and colleagues’ article “Illness identity: Capturing the influence of illness on the person’s sense of self” discusses four types of illness identity and how they can impact an individual’s ability to manage their treatment, regulate their emotions around health, and improve their quality of life.

The four types of illness identity are:

  • Engulfment: When illness dominates one’s identity and daily life
  • Rejection: When illness is minimized or kept separate from one's sense of self, often through avoidance or denial
  • Acceptance: When illness is integrated into one's self-concept and identity
  • Enrichment: When one’s illness results in positive life changes and benefits one’s identity

The research shows that quality of life is typically best for those in the acceptance and enrichment identities. Benefits include fewer depressive and anxiety symptoms, fewer physical symptoms, and the ability to manage the disease more effectively. However, it’s important to remember that these identities are fluid and can change day-to-day and situation-to-situation.

My experience with illness acceptance

It took me close to a decade to start accepting my illness in a real, honest way. I spent a long time in the rejection identity phase (see above), where I avoided acknowledging illness as part of who I was. The rejection felt safer than confronting societal norms about illness, disappointing family expectations around productivity, and navigating awkward conversations with friends about accommodations. And for a while, I could get away with rejecting illness as part of my identity.

But here’s the thing: Rejecting illness as part of my identity didn’t make it go away. What it did was lead me to reject accommodations, treatments, and emotional support that I genuinely needed. This is the danger of not integrating illness into our sense of self — it can reinforce shame and body disconnection.

So is it okay to integrate illness as part of your identity?

Absolutely.

When we integrate illness into our identity in a way that allows us to have radical acceptance and even enrich our lives, we can face the challenges that come with chronic illness more effectively. That said, it’s always worth weighing whether you are in the engulfment type of illness identity, where it’s difficult to pursue other parts of what makes you human.

No matter where you are in how you relate to your illness, you can offer yourself compassion. Identity change and integration are difficult and ongoing. You get to move at your own speed.

item.title: Why Holding Back May Be Hurting Your Relationships
item.description:
Relationships

Why Holding Back May Be Hurting Your Relationships

What do you almost say but edit out?

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • We are very skilled at recognizing the risks of oversharing.
  • We are not so good at noticing the risks of saying too little.
  • People can't connect with what they don't know about you.
  • Developing awareness for the "invisible edit" can make you a more open and vibrant person.

Every day we have conversations in our minds that never take place in real life. Maybe you hear a story and think: “That happened to me too, only in a slightly different way.” Perhaps you want to offer a compliment but stop yourself, or you recognize a vulnerability or a need in yourself or others, but almost as soon as the thought comes in, it exits, never making it past your lips. There’s a whole internal world of thoughts that may never make it to the level of a spoken sentence.

We are very good at recognizing the risks of oversharing; what we might be underestimating are the risks of revealing too little.

Leslie John, a behavioral scientist at Harvard Business School, found that we tend to focus on the risks of disclosing while underestimating the social costs of withholding. Across multiple contexts, John and her colleagues found that people often prefer those who reveal themselves over those who choose to withhold information, even when the information shared is potentially embarrassing. For example, in one study, people were more interested in going on a date with someone who answered direct questions, even when their answers were not socially desirable, than with someone who declined to answer.

Disclosing personal information, even when it’s perceived as negative, signals to the other person that you trust them enough to take that risk. That signal of trust invites openness in return, and deepens the connection. In contrast, when a person withholds and doesn’t reveal themself, it can signal a lack of trust and may then be interpreted as dishonesty, indifference, or evasiveness, even when none of those things are actually true.

There is evidence that revealing ourselves is rewarding at a neurological level. Research shows that sharing information about ourselves activates brain regions associated with reward. And from an evolutionary standpoint, attachment and connection are integral to survival.

Of course, this isn’t a reason to share everything. Boundaries are important. You don’t need to tell your boss about your marital issues or your financial situation. What is more important is to get curious about all those things that would be completely appropriate to share, and might feel good to say and for others to hear, and yet we edit out.

This is what I call the invisible edit. The invisible edit often happens without conscious awareness, but due to an internal risk sensor that almost instantaneously sends the thought to the discard bin.

Underneath that lightning-quick tendency to discard is years of cultural conditioning around not wanting to take a social risk and potentially appear awkward, needy, dramatic, weak, or foolish. Over time, we develop default versions of ourselves; versions based on an unconscious calculus of what feels safest to present in the situation at hand. This protection mechanism is so quick that it overrides a more deliberate decision of what you might be missing out on by not disclosing.

The problem is people can’t connect with what they don’t know about you.

The invisible edit is particularly harmful in long-term relationships because, over time, it can drain the aliveness and the zest of the relationship. When we stop sharing the nuance of our inner world, conversation becomes rote, and people come to occupy rigid roles.

You may think you know everything your partner feels or thinks, and they know this for you, simply because you’ve been together so long. But knowing each other a long time is not the same as revealing yourself right now in this moment. By not taking that risk or putting in that effort, you are leaving opportunities for increased closeness, joy, and softness off the table.

Slow down and recognize your inner voice and what might be getting lost in the invisible edit. For example:

When your partner does something nice for you, instead of just sticking with “thanks,” allow yourself to say: “I’m so lucky to have you care about me in this way!”

If you realize you have been letting your partner down, instead of pushing it under the rug, just say it: “I am realizing I haven’t been there for you.”

If something hurts your feelings, say: “That actually hurt.”

After a conflict, instead of just waiting it out or distracting yourself with something else, say: “I want to be close to you again.”

The goal isn’t to stop editing or to have no boundaries in what you disclose to others, but it is to build conscious awareness for the invisible edit and to be curious with yourself about why you’re editing. Then you can make a deliberate choice about whether disclosing is actually riskier than not disclosing.

Experiment today with just noticing what you almost say but don’t. What was the thought? Why did you edit it? And what might happen if you actually said it?

item.title: The Holy Grail Rule Of "Good Enough" Love In Relationships
item.description:
Relationships

The Holy Grail Rule Of "Good Enough" Love In Relationships

As it turns out, the best kind of love is actually just good enough.

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • Realistic expectations and strong conflict resolution skills lead to lasting relationship happiness.
  • Friendship and intimacy, not just passion, are key foundations for enduring love.
  • Reliability and consistent trust-building sustain long-term relationships.
  • Shared life goals create deeper purpose and connection within couples.
Source: Chermiti Mohamed / Pexels

In the quest for love and partnership, we often end up chasing after the elusive perfect match—someone who aligns seamlessly with our ideals and triggers intense passion.

Introduced by renowned psychologist and relationship researcher John Gottman, the idea of a “good enough” relationship challenges the notion of perfection and suggests that lasting love is about maintaining a balance of realistic expectations, authentic connection, and a commitment to mutual growth. This perspective flips the script on the widely held belief that flawless relationships are the ultimate goal.

“Good enough” relationships, despite their imperfections, often outlast seemingly flawless unions glorified by society. Here are three reasons why you should aim for “good enough” relationships and steps you can take toward creating one.

1. Keeping It Real Leads to Lasting Happiness

Exceptionally high standards can be detrimental for the health of a relationship in the long run. According to a study published in Personal Relationships, holding unrealistic or lofty standards for a marriage partner may lead to a tendency to delay or forgo marriage. Individuals with unrealistic standards also face greater challenges in establishing high-quality romantic relationships, express lower expectations for marrying their current partner, and exhibit lower levels of psychological and behavioral investment in the prospect of marriage.

It is essential to understand that the idea of a "good enough" relationship does not support lowering expectations to avoid disappointment or settling for being treated poorly.

A “good enough” relationship involves being treated with respect, love, and affection. Couples in such relationships recognize that occasional disappointments are inevitable, and consider their combined conflict resolution skills to be the relationship’s defining strength. By maintaining reasonable expectations, individuals set the stage for a partnership where both parties feel valued and understood.

To achieve this:

  • Foster open and honest communication to ensure a clear understanding of each other’s expectations, leading to a sense of transparency and trust.
  • Polish your indispensable conflict resolution skills to navigate disagreements constructively, averting the accumulation of lingering resentments that can erode the relationship over time.

2. Passion Invigorates, Friendship Sustains

While many concentrate on the initial stages of falling in love, fueled by attraction and shared interests, John Gottman proposes that true love encompasses more profound sentiments. In his “Sound Relationship House” theory, he asserts that couples in “good enough” relationships establish a foundation of intimacy and friendship.

Research too underlines the significance of valuing the friendship aspect of romance as a predictor of positive concurrent romantic qualities like love, sexual gratification, and commitment.

These essential ingredients act as slow-release agents that show their efficacy and impact over the course of a long-term relationship. Components of the “Sound Relationship House” theory provide a guide to fortify the foundation of intimacy through:

  • Building love maps. Delve into your partner’s inner world, comprehending them in depth.
  • Sharing fondness and admiration. Express appreciation and respect to counteract contempt.
  • Turning towards instead of away. Acknowledge and respond to your partner’s bids for connection in your daily interactions.
  • Maintaining a positive perspective. Adopt a constructive problem-solving approach, recognizing the success of repair attempts.
  • Managing conflict. Address both solvable and perpetual problems, acknowledging the natural existence of conflict.
  • Making life dreams come true. Foster an environment encouraging open communication about personal hopes, values, convictions and aspirations.
  • Creating shared meaning. Understand and embrace important visions, narratives, myths, and metaphors within the relationship.

3. Reliability Fuels Romance

Falling in love marks only the initial phase; the true test of a relationship’s mettle lies in the couple’s ability to construct and sustain trust and commitment. Couples in “good enough” relationships understand that love, to endure, must rely on intentional effort to create shared meaning and purpose. It requires ongoing dedication beyond the euphoria of the early stages.

To actively cultivate this enduring connection, prioritizing trust-building activities becomes paramount.

  • Be reliable by consistently fulfilling promises, practice transparency through open communication, and offer support during tough times by demonstrating empathy, understanding, and standing by each other when needed.
  • Establish shared life goals. This collaborative effort deepens commitment and infuses the relationship with a profound sense of purpose. The progress made leads to a shared sense of accomplishment, creating a narrative that binds a couple together and enhances the overall quality and longevity of the relationship.

In the realm of romantic relationships, the pursuit of perfection may lead to unrealistic expectations and eventual disappointment. However, embracing the concept of a “good enough” relationship, characterized by elements like respect, love, intimacy, and friendship, provides a practical roadmap to lasting happiness.
